item.title: Stock market correction? Whatever — Wall Street is bullish on 2027, and one chief investment officer sees the S&P 500 soaring 45% to 10,000
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: provides a comprehensive view of the market's outlook with clear analysis and expert opinions

The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 joined the Nasdaq in correction territory as AI stocks plunged further, but 2026 is also winding down, and Wall Street is already putting out predictions for 2027.

Analysts see solid gains ahead, with the U.S. economy expected to continue chugging along on the back of massive hyperscaler spending and resilient consumers. Some also welcomed the recent decline for taking froth off markets that might otherwise start looking overheated.

Even this week’s selloff, which marked the worst weekly loss since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic, was largely dismissed as a move driven more by emotion than fundamentals.

“This does not mean stampedes are uninformative or palpitations never presage heart attacks, but today’s panic does not feel like an AI bust,” Viktor Shvets, head of global desk strategy at Macquarie Capital, said in a note Friday.

Michael Monaghan, portfolio manager and partner at Founder ETFs, quipped that the market is “selling first and asking questions later.” And Jamie Cox, managing partner for Harris Financial Group, predicted investors will “return to rationality” and look instead to consumption-boosting GDP.

Meanwhile, Morgan Stanley chief U.S. equity strategist Michael Wilson said earlier this week that the S&P 500 would finish 2027 at 8,700, representing a 26% jump from current levels and a 15% rally when he made the call.

“We see the mid-cycle transition now ending with a more stable mid-cycle backdrop evolving in 2027,” he wrote.

Goldman Sachs also sees the broad market index soaring to 8,700 next year, “albeit with higher volatility than in recent years.”

Peter Oppenheimer, the bank’s chief global equity strategist, said that while corporate earnings growth will slow, inflation, bond yields, and oil prices will also moderate. “We expect the equity bull market to continue.”

Elsewhere, estimates were less bullish but still upbeat. UBS Global Wealth Management put the S&P 500 at 8,200 next year, implying 19% upside from Friday’s close.

Although it sees more earnings gains in 2027, Wall Street is focusing on whether the investment cycle can support profits into 2028, UBS explained.

“Cannibalization, financing, and execution risks around AI have increased while expectations and index concentration remain high,” it added. “The market is therefore more sensitive to earnings disappointment or a further rise in discount rates.”

Wells Fargo’s S&P 500 outlook in 2027 is also for 8,200, which assumes slower profit growth as well.

But then there’s Steve Chiavarone, chief investment officer for equities at Federated Hermes, who has a year-end view of 10,000—or a 45% surge from current levels.

He brushed aside this month’s midterm elections, which saw Democrats sweep Congress and several state capitals. While Wall Street fears the blue tsunami will slow the AI infrastructure boom, Chiavarone said risks to the buildout are overblown. Even a slight retreat would be positive.

“A modest pullback in the data center buildout could give cash flows time to catch up, easing inflation pressures and making the investment boom more sustainable,” he argued.

Slower prices could prevent additional rate hikes from the Federal Reserve, which has grown more hawkish as policymakers become impatient with inflation exceeding their 2% target for over five years.

Although Wall Street sees more tightening in the coming months, some analysts also anticipate rate cuts later in 2027 as inflation cools. But that assumes the Iran war will be over some time next year.

For now, Gaurav Mallik, chief investment officer at Modera Wealth Management, described the market slide as a “garden variety correction,” with stock leadership rotating from tech to industrials and financials.

“The pullback in stocks sets the market up nicely for 2027, which we believe will be a high-single-digit year,” he added. “Multiples are shrinking, and total returns are a function of earnings growth, which so far looks robust for 2027.”

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-22 00:02 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: The AI bust is a growing threat to China’s economy and a ‘moment of real danger’ for President Xi Jinping, analyst warns
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: addresses a significant economic issue with relevant context and analysis

U.S. investors are facing a meltdown in tech stocks and the possible end of the AI boom, but the bubble has already popped in China, where an even worse market crash threatens the economy and President Xi Jinping, according to Yardeni Research.

China’s tech-heavy STAR 50 index has tumbled 44% from its high this summer, while the Nasdaq is down 18% from its record—even after U.S. stocks suffered their worst week since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic.

That’s thrown a wrench into Xi’s plans for the economy, Yardeni said in a note earlier this month. While the Chinese leader was riding high as host to global leaders this week, the market’s downturn jeopardizes his plan to turn China’s savers into stock investors who can finance the AI buildout and de-emphasize the property market.

Real estate accounts for roughly 70% of household wealth in China and was traditionally a place to stash savings. But the housing crash has weighed on consumer demand, even producing intermittent deflation. Business investment is also falling, with October data showing property investment sank nearly 22%.

With the domestic market still weak, Beijing has instead relied on a flood of cheap exports to keep the economy growing while also deploying the “national team” of state-backed banks to pump money into the stock market.

But according to Yardeni, Chinese stocks collapsed this year due in part to cutthroat competition, heavier tax burdens, higher energy costs, tariffs, and the risk that China’s trading partners will block exports being sold at ultra-low prices.

“To keep AI funding flowing, Xi needs a buoyant stock market,” the note said. “Otherwise, AI risks being folded into the state-owned enterprise (SOE) universe that his team has pledged to shrink since 2013, further crowding out the private sector.”

Retail investors are also skittish about Chinese stocks after Xi’s government cracked down on the tech sector in 2020. The market’s reputation as a rigged casino that favors politically connected insiders doesn’t help either. In fact, the Shanghai Composite remains well below its October 2007 peak despite China’s GDP exploding nearly sixfold.

Many households now have “financial PTSD” after repeated stock busts, including a crash in the summer of 2015 that required an aggressive national team rescue, Yardeni added.

To be sure, China remains a leader in AI, and mom-and-pop investors still drive most of the trade, even as they treat the market more like high-stakes gambling than a place to grow retirement savings.

“Yet this is a moment of real danger for Xi. A bursting AI bubble would not merely erase wealth or dent China’s technological prestige. It would weaken Beijing’s attempt to replace a broken property model with a stock-market-led one,” Yardeni warned.

“China can build world-class AI models, train engineers, and spend billions on chips. But if its households still view Shanghai as a casino with odds set by the Politburo, Xi’s dream of creating a Chinese version of Wall Street may remain just that: a dream.”

Underscoring its importance to Beijing, Premier Li Qiang told a State Council executive meeting earlier this month that stabilizing capital markets was the top priority for the rest of the year.

It followed securities regulators sharply easing requirements for company buybacks that help lift stock prices and discouraging IPOs and large share sales to prevent stock dilution that triggers selloffs.

But the spy scandal that dethroned Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia represents a new risk to China’s AI ambitions. Backlash over the advanced U.S. chips and computing capacity that China had access to has spurred the Trump administration to impose new technology curbs.

“By targeting both indirect chip shipments to China and its access to overseas computing power, the new controls threaten to slow the catch-up of China’s leading AI models and to slow China’s AI rollout,” analysts at Capital Economics wrote on Tuesday.

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-21 21:45 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: highlights the significant IPO of an AI giant with market impact

Investors scramble for a piece of AI giant Anthropic in blockbuster IPO

AI giant Anthropic raises more than $100 billion in record-setting IPO

Shares in the artificial intelligence giant Anthropic soared in their market debut after the company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering and private placement that valued it at around $1.5 trillion.

It's a remarkably rapid ascent for the five-year-old AI company, and a sign of strong investor appetite despite growing concern about a possible AI bubble.

Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share.

The company's seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic's prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.

The total haul is more than $107 billion.

The amount of money raised makes Anthropic's IPO the biggest in history, after Elon Musk's mega-conglomerate SpaceX landed $75 billion when it listed in June.

Anthropic's shares opened trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT at $111.50, a whopping 34% above the IPO price. They eased over the trading day to end 17% higher at $97.17.

A breakaway beginning

Anthropic's rise has been meteoric.

"We've never seen a company that's able to grow this fast [and] be this dominant," said Andrew Rocco, a stock analyst at the financial research firm Zacks.

Anthropic got its start in 2021 as a breakaway group of researchers who once worked for ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. Led by now-CEO Dario Amodei, the Anthropic founders were concerned that OpenAI, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.

Amodei and the others quickly raised hundreds of millions of dollars and set out to develop AI models in a way that the company said focused on safety and "alignment," or the idea that AI should be harmless and act in ways that jibe with human values and intent.

Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, just months after OpenAI released ChatGPT. Ever since, the two companies have been neck-and-neck competitors in cutting-edge artificial intelligence, known as "frontier AI." The Claude family of AI models, including the Claude chatbot and Claude Code, are among the most popular and powerful in the world, and have helped transform everything from online search to software engineering.

They are also the San Francisco-based company's main source of income, according to its IPO prospectus, which said revenue in the first half of the year skyrocketed 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, versus a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.

Opportunities and risks

The IPO comes at a time when shares in tech companies linked to the AI boom have been volatile. Investors have vacillated between enthusiasm for what many believe will be a revolutionary technology and concern that the vast sums of money being poured into it may be hard to justify.

"It's going to be a test of investor sentiment towards the AI trade," said Janice Quek, an equity analyst at the investment research firm CFRA. "We've seen in recent weeks that there has been a lot of pressure and really market sell-offs on the AI ecosystem just because a lot of people are worried about the AI bubble, for example, or the concerns around AI financing and whether there's a return on investment on AI."

The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October.

Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, told a Semafor conference on Monday the IPO is one of the best ways to invest in AI applications. He said his firm had trimmed its exposure to AI infrastructure — companies involved in things like manufacturing semiconductors and building data centers — but that Altimeter had requested an allotment of Anthropic stock worth $5 billion.

"I've been waiting for it," he said of the IPO. "We put in for the largest request in the 20-year history of our firm."

There is indirect evidence in Anthropic's prospectus that businesses, rather than individual subscribers, are its biggest source of revenue. Malik Ahmed Khan, an equity analyst at Morningstar, says the company's long-term success may hinge on those companies' pace of adoption of AI technologies, but it's unclear how fast that will be.

"Radios went from like 10% penetration to 90% penetration in the U.S. within a decade. Washing machines, to reach that level of penetration, took a multi-decade period," he said. "So when we're thinking about Anthropic and broadly AI in the enterprise setting, what does that adoption curve look like?"

Conflict with the Pentagon, and "pacing the frontier"

Anthropic has not been without controversy. Earlier this year it became embroiled in a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. The Pentagon wanted the military to be able to deploy Anthropic's models without restriction, but Amodei drew a line at fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon subsequently labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk," a designation previously reserved for foreign adversaries.

And skeptics have criticized Amodei's rapid push to develop AI despite his own dire warnings about the technology's risks. In September, Amodei wrote an essay urging his AI competitors to "pace the frontier," or to slow down development of the most cutting-edge models and make sure that safety incidents are being reported and scrutinized by third-party auditors.

On Thursday, Amodei said the company's principles would not change.…

Source: NPR Business | Published: 2026-11-19 10:00 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.npr.org/2026/11/19/nx-s1-6042558/anthropic-ipo-breaks-records-100-billion

item.title: Even FEMA officials are worried about the string of outages and withdrew extra cash — ‘This is scary, and there is no leadership’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: explores a critical issue in emergency response with depth and detail

The Trump administration has insisted that the recent surge in network outages isn’t due to a cyberattack, but those responsible for the federal government’s emergency response aren’t so sure.

Two officials at the Federal Emergency Management Agency told the Washington Post they were concerned about the outages and were having trouble believing they were a coincidence.

One official took out extra cash, and the other reported being bombarded with questions from former classmates asking whether they should prepare for an emergency.

“There is nothing on this scale that has happened before in this many sectors this close together,” one of the officials told the Post. “This is scary, and there is no leadership.”

FEMA didn’t respond to a request for comment.

Even before everything appeared to break down, Americans were already on edge after the Pentagon launched an initiative called FORTRESS, which seeks to ensure that every major U.S. military base can run for 90 days without outside help if a war cuts off power and supply chains.

Then came a month of cyberattacks that hit hundreds of companies and institutions around the world. The hacking spree was so widespread that it was dubbed “Black October.” The Nvidia spy scandal also didn’t help sentiment.

Last Thursday, Microsoft’s email and other office tools went down. Last Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration grounded all planes for more than four hours. It later blamed a copper wire that was being upgraded to a fiber-optic cable.

Days later, companies like Chase, Wells Fargo, United Airlines, and Apple saw temporary service disruptions. The National Security Agency’s internal classified communications network also suffered an outage, further fraying nerves.

U.S. officials have said there’s no evidence of cyberattacks, suggesting network upgrades meant to patch newly uncovered vulnerabilities were deployed hastily before all the bugs were worked out.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton told the House Homeland Security Committee on Wednesday that “these are separate service outages associated with maintenance and technical changes. They are not a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.”

Despite the administration’s denials that cybersecurity was an issue, the White House removed U.S. National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross on Thursday. CNN also reported Friday that said the FBI is investigating an apparent breach of its nationwide criminal information database—the second such breach in recent months.

The steady drumbeat of alarming news has pushed many Americans into panic mode. Costco and Walmart have seen more shoppers stocking up on emergency supplies.

“Consumer anxiety, following the Microsoft Outlook outage, the ground stoppage for all U.S. airline flights, and apocalyptic concerns flaring up across social media, have all contributed to increased emergency prep sales at Costco,” Mizuho analyst David Bellinger wrote in a recent note.

Adding to the unease was the U.K. government’s campaign urging Britons to keep canned food, bottled water, and cash on hand to get through three days of disruption.

And for good measure, the stock market has been pummeled with some of the worst declines since the early days of the COVID-19 pandemic as investors fear the end of the AI boom could take the U.S. economy down with it.

The cumulative effect of all the disruptions has caused Americans to fear the worst. Chuck Amasio, a 68-year-old from Rahway, New Jersey, who was stuck at Newark Liberty International Airport, told the Associated Press last week “there’s a lot of weird stuff going on” and wondered if it was all part of some form of attack.

“We talk about how wars aren’t done with bombs anymore,” he added. “They shut down airspace or a power grid. They can cripple an economy.”

But in an interview with Fortune’s Catherina Gioino, Mark Giles, director of Downdetector parent company Ookla Research, said there’s nothing linking the outages.

“This is a big blip, but it’s kind of on par for the course for what we’re seeing in terms of those longer-term trends,” he explained. “Most of the time they’re fairly self-contained and remedied quite quickly. It’s the ones where you can’t withdraw money or you can’t access your emails that really get the headlines.”

Source: Fortune | Published: 2026-11-21 18:50 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://fortune.com/2026/11/21/fema-network-outages-extra-cash-emergency-supplies-cyberattacks/

item.title: Canada could work with Chinese automakers if US trade talks fail, says Carney
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: addresses a potential shift in the auto industry with international implications

The prime minister of Canada, Mark Carney, said the country could turn to Chinese automakers if trade negotiations with the US president, Donald Trump, failed to preserve an integrated North American auto industry.

Carney’s comments in Cambodia on Monday came ahead of a planned meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week in Shenzhen, China, where auto manufacturing is expected to be discussed. The two leaders reached an agreement in January allowing tens of thousands of Chinese electric vehicles into Canada at reduced tariffs.

“We have the best auto workers in the world, and we want them fully deployed, full opportunity, in an integrated North American market,” Carney told reporters in Cambodia. “That market has become less integrated because of US trade actions.”

He said on Monday that negotiations with the US remained his priority, but their outcome could determine whether Canada pursues alternatives involving European, Chinese or Japanese automakers. A day earlier in Manila, in the Philippines, Carney said any trade agreement with Washington must leave Canada with a viable auto industry.

Asked whether potential Chinese investment was leverage in US negotiations, Carney replied: “It’s not leverage. But action, reaction.

“If they [Canada’s auto workers] are not fully utilized in a North American context, that provides other opportunities,” Carney said. “Canada is going to move forward either way.”

The Detroit Three – Ford, General Motors and Stellantis – operate factories across Canada, the US and Mexico, with parts sometimes crossing borders multiple times before a vehicle is completed. Trump has repeatedly pushed automakers to move production to the US from Canada.

Carney said any Chinese investment would have to involve substantial manufacturing in Canada rather than simply assembling imported parts. He said it would need proper labor standards, manufacturing facilities and domestic supply chains that expand over time, including Canadian critical minerals used in electric vehicles.

“It’s not just about kit cars,” he said. “There has to be a manufacturing aspect involved.”

Under a January agreement, Canada reduced its 100% tariff on Chinese electric vehicles to 6.1%, initially allowing up to 49,000 vehicles annually, with the cap increasing over time. In exchange, China agreed to lower tariffs on Canadian agricultural products, including canola.

Carney said at the time that he expected the agreement to attract Chinese investment in Canada’s auto industry and create jobs.

The deal drew criticism from Ontario premier Doug Ford, whose province is the center of Canada’s auto industry. Ford warned that allowing Chinese electric vehicles into Canada could threaten Canadian jobs and jeopardize access to the US market.

Trump’s tariffs have disrupted Canada’s auto industry, which relies heavily on cross-border production. Canada recently threatened to sue Stellantis after the automaker shifted planned Jeep Compass production from Brampton, Ontario, to Illinois and agreed to sell its idled Canadian assembly plant.

Carney said Saturday that he had spoken at length with Trump and senior US officials and that the two countries were making progress toward a possible trade agreement, although differences remained.

Source: The Guardian Business | Published: 2026-11-16 04:39 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

Original link: https://www.theguardian.com/world/2026/nov/16/canada-carney-cars-evs-tariffs-xi-jinping-china-trump-trade-talks

item.title: Megaspeed, the company linked to the downfall of Nvidia boss, says it’s a ‘legitimate and lawful business’
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: investigates a significant corporate event with implications for the tech industry

Megaspeed International, the company linked to the downfall of the Nvidia chief, Jensen Huang, says it is a “legitimate and lawful business” and has announced that its director, who allegedly had an affair with Jensen Huang, left the business in late 2025.

The Singapore-based cloud computing company on the weekend said it was “aware of recent media reports containing assertions about our business, supply chain and global operations that are not supported by verifiable evidence”.

Megaspeed said it had “retained external legal counsel to conduct a thorough internal investigation”.

Jensen Huang resigned as chief executive of the chip manufacturer Nvidia after reports of extramarital affairs with Alice Huang and two company employees.

US intelligence agencies believe the tech chief, whose products have been crucial to the AI boom, had been targeted by Alice Huang, the former director of Megaspeed International.

US officials have alleged Alice Huang may have been acting as a Chinese intelligence asset, passing commercial information to Beijing, the New York Times has reported.

In the past three years, Megaspeed has been one of Nvidia’s biggest foreign customers, buying nearly US$5bn (A$7.4bn, £3.8bn) in AI chips and advanced hardware.

A US senator asked the commerce department to investigate whether Megaspeed had diverted Nvidia chips to China.

Megaspeed said on Sunday it would not comment on Alice Huang’s “personal and private matters”.

“Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the company,” it said in a statement.

The global facades of Megaspeed International form a puzzling corporate picture, and involve a lottery retailer in rural Australia, a dilapidated storefront in Kuala Lumpur and a near-empty office in Singapore.

The company on Sunday said: “Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate.”

Short seller Culper Research in May quoted a Megaspeed employee as saying Alice Huang was “still our boss”, in a report accusing Nvidia of having a “China problem”.

On Thursday, Singaporean authorities said Alice Huang had been barred from re-entering the city state after a 2025 investigation into the company’s “suspected breaches of our domestic laws”.

The ministry of home affairs said it had held Alice Huang’s passport from June 2025 until February. Police believed she had given them “inaccurate” information, to downplay her role at the company, but released her due to insufficient evidence.

She was issued a stern warning and barred from re-entering the country. Taiwan has also barred her from re-entry, its authorities have said.

Singapore’s initial investigation related to Megaspeed’s potential “false declarations” over the purchase of computer servers.

On Friday, Malaysia said it was investigating a subsidiary of Megaspeed International over the possible diversion of advanced AI chips to other countries.

Megaspeed has previously said there was no evidence of illegal chip transfers.

Its registered Sydney office is home to numerous business and had no Megaspeed signage, mailbox or physical presence when the Guardian visited last week. No one had heard of Megaspeed Australia or its listed director, 29-year-old Kai Kang.

Reuters visited a news agency and lottery retailer, in Seymour, Victoria, an hour’s drive north of Melbourne, where a woman, who identified herself as Kang’s mother, said Kang was based in Shanghai and did not know anything about the Singaporean company.

Kang has not been accused of any wrongdoing. Attempts to contact him were unsuccessful.

The US attorney general, Todd Blanche, said last week that the Justice Department had not concluded whether Alice Huang was a Chinese spy.

Asked whether she was a spy, the US president, Donald Trump, said: “I don’t know if that’s been determined yet.”

Beijing rejected the allegations as unsubstantiated. Associated Press was unable to reach Alice Huang for comment. The Guardian has sought comment from Alice Huang.

Megaspeed began as the overseas arm of a Chinese video game developer and was incorporated in Singapore in 2015 as 7Road International. It adopted its current name in March 2023, when all its shares were transferred to Huang Le Limited, a British Virgin Islands company. Alice Huang is also known by her Chinese name, Huang Le.

By November 2023, she was no longer listed as a Megaspeed director, and all her shares had been transferred to an entity owned by Singaporean businessman Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan.

The company’s finances have also attracted attention. Singapore corporate records show its total assets rose roughly 90-fold from end-2023 to 2024, reaching almost US$3bn (A$4.4bn, £2.3bn).

Source: The Guardian Business | Published: 2026-11-16 01:17 UTC | Difficulty: 61/100

item.title: When the boss has an affair, the whole family business can pay the price
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: examines the personal and professional consequences of a high-profile affair

From Profumo to Petraeus to Gary Hart, Bill Gates and Bill Clinton, history is littered with older men in positions of great responsibility having affairs with mostly younger women that put their jobs, businesses and reputations at great risk. Now we have the former Nvidia CEO, Jensen Huang.

These men – smart, respected, powerful – make decisions that simply baffle the rest of us. If they’re so intelligent, how could they not see how things were going to end up? The answer is they’re men. And when there’s a younger woman who shows interest, well …

We all love a bit of schadenfreude now and again. But it’s not so fun for the employees, shareholders, partners and others who work alongside these men. And it’s deeply unpleasant for their families, particularly when they work in the same business.

Jensen Huang’s family is feeling that right now. His son, daughter and son-in-law all have prominent positions at his company. His daughter is married to another Nvidia executive. And they’re not alone. And when it happens at a smaller business, the impact is even worse.

Huang’s company is so well known that the world knows of his indiscretions. But people live in their own worlds, and in my client’s world, pretty much everyone in the company knows what’s going on with the cheating spouse.

Some surveys claim that as many as 20% of people have admitted to cheating on their partners. There are 34m small businesses in the US with almost a third being family owned. So the odds are that there are other moms and dads (probably dads, given that 61% of businesses are still owned by men) making the same mistakes. I have clients in this position. And their children working in their businesses are going through the same horrible experience.

Hopefully, the children working in family businesses have positions where they are not directly reporting to mom and dad. Hopefully there’s an organizational structure and policies in place that separates them from ownership and treats them as any other employee. Whether the owner of the company – even if it’s the mom or dad (again probably the dad) – is having dalliances on the side should be of no matter. They’re doing a job in the company. They’re not a part of this.

But unfortunately they are. It’s still their parents. There’s still an unsaid thing amongst the rest of the employees that not only are they the kids but they’re also likely to be the future owners of the company. Their behavior inside the company walls is being watched as closely as their parents. Suddenly, their parents’ behavior is now reflected on them. Can they also be trusted?

And yet I don’t feel entirely sorry for the Jensen kids or any kids working for their parents where a similar situation occurs. They’ve enjoyed the perks of being the owners’ offspring. They’ve likely been given opportunities they wouldn’t necessarily get if they worked for someone else. They know what they signed up for.

The hope is that Huang’s children, and the children of any business owner going through the same situation, learn and turn it to their favor. When a responsible CEO cheats on their spouse, it calls into question their overall ethics. When the affairs become a circus like Jensen’s – or even in the smaller world of my clients – the ridicule it creates undermines their authority. People look at my cheating clients like they’re a joke. They wonder how they could do something so blatantly stupid like having an affair with an employee in an environment where their children work? They question the judgment of the very leader who runs the company that provides their livelihood.
